---
title: "Regular GLM models"
description: "Sparse examples for the standard R GLM families and two Gamma variance models."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
library(L0glm)
```

Supply the same family object you would use in `glm()`. These examples use
a common design with three active predictors and a GIC penalty. An
unpenalized intercept is included in each fit. The helper returns the
selected predictor indices, with indexing starting at the first column of
`X`.

```{r design}
set.seed(34)
n <- 300L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 20L), n, 20L)
eta <- 0.4 + 0.6 * X[, 2] - 0.5 * X[, 7] + 0.4 * X[, 12]
fit <- function(y, family) {
  l0glmFit(X, y, family=family, intercept=TRUE, lambda="gic", relaxed=TRUE)
}
selected <- function(model) which(as.numeric(coef(model))[-1L] != 0)
```

## Gaussian and quasi with constant variance

Use an identity link for a sparse linear model. A quasi family lets you
specify a link and variance function directly. Here a constant variance
gives the same mean model as Gaussian regression.

```{r gaussian}
y <- eta + rnorm(n, sd=0.5)
gaussian_fit <- fit(y, gaussian())
quasi_fit <- fit(y, quasi(link="identity", variance="constant"))
selected(gaussian_fit)
selected(quasi_fit)
```

## Binomial and quasibinomial

A binary response can be given as zeroes and ones. For proportions
calculated from trial counts, pass the number of trials as weights.
Quasibinomial allows extra variability around the binomial mean.

```{r binomial}
prob <- plogis(1.5 * eta)
binary <- fit(rbinom(n, 1, prob), binomial())
trials <- rep(12, n)
successes <- rbinom(n, trials, plogis(qlogis(prob) + rnorm(n, sd=0.5)))
quasi_binary <- l0glmFit(X, successes / trials, weights=trials,
  family=quasibinomial(), intercept=TRUE, lambda="gic", relaxed=TRUE)
selected(binary)
selected(quasi_binary)
```

## Poisson and quasipoisson

The log link gives multiplicative effects on the mean. With quasipoisson,
the variance is a fitted or supplied multiple of the mean. The
[negative binomial tutorial](negative-binomial.html) covers two likelihood
models for overdispersed counts.

```{r poisson}
mu <- exp(eta)
counts <- fit(rpois(n, mu), poisson())
overdispersed <- fit(rnbinom(n, mu=mu, size=2), quasipoisson())
selected(counts)
selected(overdispersed)
```

## Gamma with fixed shape or common scale

Use `Gamma(link="log")` for positive continuous responses with
\(\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi\mu_i^2\). Its Gamma shape is \(1/\phi\).
Use `gammaScale()` when the variance is proportional to the mean. It
uses a common scale \(b\), shape \(\mu_i/b\), and variance \(b\mu_i\).

```{r gamma}
fixed_shape <- fit(rgamma(n, shape=8, scale=mu / 8), Gamma(link="log"))
b <- 0.2
common_scale <- fit(rgamma(n, shape=mu / b, scale=b), gammaScale(scale=b))
selected(fixed_shape)
selected(common_scale)
```

When recorded zeroes denote intensities below a detection limit,
`gammaCensored(dispersion=1/8, censor=0.5)` retains the fixed-shape model
and includes those observations through their lower-tail probabilities.
`gammaScale()` also accepts a detection limit. [Signal families reference](../reference/signal_families.html)

## Inverse Gaussian

This model is useful for positive outcomes whose variance grows cubically
with the mean, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi\mu_i^3\).

```{r inverse-gaussian}
duration <- statmod::rinvgauss(n, mean=mu, dispersion=0.08)
inverse_gaussian <- fit(duration, inverse.gaussian(link="log"))
selected(inverse_gaussian)
predict(inverse_gaussian, X[1:4, ], type="response")
```

See the [R family reference](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/family.html)
for the available links and the [model selection tutorial](selection.html)
for tuning by information criteria or cross-validation.
